title: The three types of machine learning
intro: Supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement? The three families of machine learning, what data each of them needs, which tasks belong to them — and how two questions tell you which family your problem is.

blocks.html: Machine learning is classified by the kind of feedback the model learns from. Do you have examples with answers? That is supervised learning. Do you only have data without answers and are you looking for structure? That is unsupervised learning. And if a program learns by acting and receiving rewards, it is called reinforcement learning.

In practice — and on this entire site — supervised learning is by far the most used: it is what scikit-learn describes as “fit on (X, y)”. But you will meet the two other families everywhere in the field, so they belong in your basic vocabulary.

sections.title: Supervised learning: learning with the answer attached

blocks.html: In supervised learning your data consists of pairs: the features X (what you know) and the target y (the answer). The model learns the mapping from X to y, so that later it can also predict a y for new X. Within this family there are two tasks, distinguished by what kind of y you predict.

rows: MSE, RMSE, MAE, R² — see the Evaluation & metrics chapter

blocks.html: Note the terminology: classification with two classes is called binary; with three or more classes it is multi-class (chapter 3 goes deeper). And “regression” in “logistic regression” is confusing: despite the name it is a classification algorithm — the regression step happens under the hood.
The hallmark of supervised learning: you already have the answer for your training data. The model learns the relation, not the answer itself — and is then tested on questions it has not seen yet.

Sometimes you have no answers — only data. Unsupervised learning then looks for structure: clustering groups similar samples (KMeans is the classic), dimensionality reduction compresses many columns into a few (PCA), and anomaly detection flags the points that belong nowhere. A typical application: customer segmentation — discover for yourself which groups of customers exist in your sales data.

Below is a minimal example: eight points in two dimensions that clearly form two groups. KMeans finds the two groups without anyone ever telling it what the groups are. Feel free to run the code in your browser.

blocks.caption: KMeans finds structure without labels
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# 8 points in 2D — two visible groups
X = np.array([[1, 2], [1.5, 1.8], [1.2, 2.2],
              [8, 9], [8.5, 8.8], [8.2, 9.3],
              [1.1, 1.9], [8.8, 9.1]])

km = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print('cluster per point :', km.labels_)
print('centres           :', km.cluster_centers_.round(1))
print('point [2, 2]      -> cluster', km.predict([[2, 2]])[0],
      '(belongs to the bottom-left group)')

blocks.html: In unsupervised learning there is no y to check against — the quality of a clustering is judged by you, by interpreting the groups. That is exactly why it is called “learning without a teacher”.

In reinforcement learning (RL) an agent learns by acting in an environment: every action yields a (delayed) reward or penalty, and the agent optimises its policy to maximise the total reward. There is no labelled example of “the right move” — only the long-term outcome. Famous results: AlphaGo, robot control, and the RLHF technique used to fine-tune large language models.

The difference from supervised learning is essential: in supervised learning you get the correct answer for each example; in RL you must discover which actions led to the reward yourself — and the reward often comes much later. Think of chess: you only find out at the end whether you won.

rows: “I have examples with the correct answer.”
“I only have data and am looking for structure or groups.”

blocks.html: These two questions — “do you have labels?” and “does the feedback come per example or via rewards?” — place almost every ML system in the right family. A handy tool for assignments and exams.
